title: AI delivers 'zero financial payoff' to most companies, Apollo economist says
content:
AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch).
Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity.
“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said.
Is this simply a matter of non-tech companies lagging behind the tech giants? Slok sounded skeptical, arguing that it will be tough for corporate America to “turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.”
“AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote, later adding, “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.”
Recent studies have also found that AI has yet to deliver significant productivity gains.

report.summary: Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok says AI has produced no measurable profit or productivity gains for the S&P 493, arguing business intelligence is really judgment.
report.background: The note lands in the middle of an unprecedented capital expenditure cycle: hyperscalers and chipmakers have poured hundreds of billions into data centers, GPUs and model training, and AI has been the dominant driver of US equity returns. Slok's framing — the 'S&P 493,' meaning the S&P 500 minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla — is a way of isolating the companies that buy AI rather than sell it. His finding echoes the classic Solow productivity paradox, in which computers appeared everywhere except in the productivity statistics. It also follows a wave of enterprise pilots that failed to scale, surveys showing generative AI adoption concentrated in narrow tasks like drafting and summarization, and earlier academic and consultancy studies that found little or no aggregate productivity effect so far, despite optimistic long-run forecasts.
key_points: The core claim rests on a deliberately narrow sample: the S&P 500 minus the seven companies that build and sell most AI. For those 493 firms, profit margins and revenue per worker look flat, with no visible uptick that can be attributed to AI adoption.

The mismatch is stark. Trillions in announced investment and relentless vendor marketing sit against no aggregate financial evidence of return outside tech, which undermines the assumption that spending on AI automatically converts into earnings power.

Slok is skeptical that laggards will simply catch up. Making intelligence cheap, he argues, does not by itself produce higher revenue growth or fatter margins — the hard part is reorganizing processes, incentives and products around it.

His sharpest point is philosophical: AI is a great calculator, but business runs on judgment. Accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules and ethical trade-offs shape reputation and margins, and models do not grasp them.

The note is not isolated. Recent studies and enterprise surveys have similarly found limited measurable productivity gains, adding weight to the argument that AI's economic payoff is real but slow, uneven and hard to attribute.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes the debate from capability to return on investment. Expect investors and boards to demand harder evidence linking AI spend to revenue, margin or headcount metrics, which will pressure vendors selling horizontal copilots and favor tools tied to specific, measurable workflows. For developers, the lesson is that model quality is no longer the bottleneck — integration, data plumbing, evaluation and change management are, and those are where value gets captured. For regular users, the practical near-term effect may be quieter: fewer dramatic productivity claims, more AI embedded invisibly in existing software, and slower visible change in jobs than the hype cycle implied.
report.tools: If you want to measure AI's actual payoff rather than assume it, look at evaluation and observability stacks: LangSmith and Langfuse for tracing LLM applications, Braintrust and OpenAI Evals for systematic testing, Weights & Biases Weave for experiment tracking, and Arize Phoenix for production monitoring. Pair these with cost-per-task dashboards and before/after workflow time studies, so you can attribute gains to specific use cases instead of aggregate vibes.
